text: Ranuccio Bianchi Bandinelli (19 February 1900 – 17 January 1975) was an Italian archaeologist and art historian. He was born in Siena to Mario Bianchi Bandinelli (1859–1930) and Margherita Ottilie "Lily" von Korn (Bianchi Bandinelli, 1878–1905), both of whom were descended from ancient aristocracy in Siena. His early research focused on the Etruscan centers near his family lands, Clusium in 1925 and Suana in 1929. Despite having shown Hitler around Rome under Mussolini, he became disillusioned with Italian fascism and converted to communism after World War II, becoming a Marxist. In 1945, he co-founded the magazine Società with Cesare Luporini and Romano Bilenchi. As an anti-fascist, he was appointed to several key art-historical positions after the war, including director of the government's fine arts and antiquities ministry (Antichità e Belle Arti) from 1945 to 1948. His memoir on fascism in Italy, titled Hitler e Mussolini, 1938: il viaggio del Führer in Italia, was published in 1995. From his positions at the universities of Florence and Rome, he guided a new generation of Italian archaeologists grounded in dialectical materialism, and he also taught at the University of Groningen in the Netherlands. In the 1950s and 1960s, he wrote comprehensive texts on classical art for a broad, literate audience. In 1958, he founded the Enciclopedia dell'arte antica and was elected a foreign member of the Soviet Academy of Sciences that same year. In the mid-1960s, he was commissioned to write two volumes on Roman art for the French Arts of Mankind series, which expanded his influence and introduced social criteria for art to a wider, English-speaking audience. In 1967, he founded the Dialoghi di archeologia with his students, a highly innovative and controversial journal in classical archaeology. He was frequently a maverick in his interpretations, with arguments that were not always convincing but were forcefully grounded. For example, regarding the Belvedere Apollo—a Roman copy of a Greek work now believed to date to the fourth century B.C.—he argued it was a frigid copy of a Hellenistic work unrelated to the Greek master Leochares, contrary to the mainstream view. His work emphasized the interrelation between Hellenistic, Etruscan, and Roman art. Among his students were influential 20th-century Italian archaeologists, including Giovanni Becatti, Antonio Giuliano, Mario Torelli, Andrea Carandini, and Filippo Coarelli. He was elected a foreign member of the Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences in 1966.
